blocks.sourceSectionTitle: The section order that actually works for freshers

rows: Contact line
Name, phone, email, city, LinkedIn URL, and a portfolio/GitHub link if relevant. No photo, no age, no marital status.
Summary (2-3 lines, not an "objective")
Degree, strongest skill area, and one specific thing you have built or done. Written for the exact role, not copy-pasted across applications.
Skills
Grouped by type (languages, tools, frameworks, soft skills) in a plain comma-separated line, not a graphic skill bar.
Projects
Your strongest 2-4 projects, each with the problem, what you built, tools used, and one measurable outcome.
Internships (if any)
Even a 4-6 week internship goes here, written with the same outcome-first structure as a job.
Education
Degree, institution, year, and CGPA/percentage only if it is a genuine strength.

blocks.heading: Formatting Basics Recruiters and Bots Both Need
blocks.sourceSectionTitle: ATS formatting basics recruiters and bots both need

rows: File format

.docx is the safest, most universally parsed format for ATS systems used by large recruiters. A well-tagged PDF exported from a simple layout also works in most modern ATS, but avoid PDFs built from heavily designed templates.
Layout
Single column, no text boxes, no tables for layout, no headers/footers containing your name or contact details. ATS parsers frequently fail to read text placed inside these elements.
Fonts and formatting
Stick to standard fonts (Calibri, Arial, or similar) and use bold/italics sparingly for emphasis, not for entire sections.
Section headings
Use plain, standard headings the parser recognizes: "Skills", "Projects", "Experience", "Education". Creative headings like "My Journey" or "What I Bring" often get skipped by parsing software.
Keywords
Mirror the exact terms from the job description where genuinely true of your background. If the listing says "React.js", write "React.js", not just "React" or "frontend development".
Graphics and icons
Skill-bar graphics, star ratings, and icon-based contact rows are invisible to most ATS parsing engines, so the information inside them is effectively lost from your applicant record.

blocks.heading: One Page or Two Pages
blocks.sourceSectionTitle: One page or two pages: the honest answer

rows: Genuinely no internships, 2-3 solid projects, standard coursework
One page. A one-page resume for a fresher signals clarity of thinking; padding it to two pages usually adds noise, not proof.
One or more internships, 4+ strong projects, relevant certifications
Still fits one page for most freshers if you cut ruthlessly. Keep only the strongest 2-4 projects and the most relevant internship detail.
Multiple internships, published work, competition wins, and leadership roles
A tight second page is acceptable if every line on it earns its place. A half-full second page reads worse than a full first page.
Campus placement portal or a large-company ATS submission
Default to one page unless the specific portal instructions say otherwise. Most fresher-level ATS workflows are built around a single-page scan.

blocks.heading: Projects Section That Pulls Its Weight

items.text: Name the problem first.
Name the tools honestly.
End with a result.
Listing every course from your syllabus, including generic ones every student in your program also took.
"Member, college coding club" with no context on what that involvement actually produced.
Hobbies listed without any connection to the role you are applying for.
Scale: dataset size, number of users, number of test cases, number of pages, number of items processed.
Accuracy or performance: model accuracy, load time improvement, error rate reduction, even at a small, honest scale.
Rank or recognition: hackathon placement, competition standing, shortlist or finalist status.
Reach: people who used, viewed, or attended something you built or organized.
Time or effort: duration of the project, team size you coordinated, number of iterations you shipped.
